Subnetting!

Subnetting is an important process for companies. It provides network rationalization and prevent from congestion. Let’s understand how…

Subnetting is an important process for companies. It provides network rationalization and prevent from congestion:

Case 1: Subnetting allows allocating properly IP addresses to prevent from large amounts of IP addresses going unused.

Case 2: If you have a lot of traffic flowing between particular parts of your network, subnetting is a way to organize the traffic to make it quicker and more direct in routing (avoid congestion).

Let's see how to design subnets practically.

Device identifiers

To understand the subnetting process, you need to know some fundamentals of networking: in networking, devices are identified by MAC (Media Access Controller) addresses and IP (Internet Protocol) addresses.

Let's start to understand them!

MAC address

A MAC (Media Access Control) address, is a unique identifier assigned to a network interface controller (NIC) for use as a network address in communications within a network segment.

MAC addresses are typically represented as six groups of two hexadecimal digits, separated by hyphens, colons, or without a separator.

For example, a MAC address might look like this:

00:0a:95:9d:68:16

MAC addresses are assigned by the manufacturer of the NIC. This means that every NIC in the world has a unique MAC address.

MAC address are typically used in local network (LAN) to allow switches to filter data sent through the network based on the MAC address. However, using MAC address requires central appliance in the network which is not possible on the internet.

So instead, the internet uses IP addresses and routing process.

Illustration of a communication based on MAC address:

IP address

IP address identifies the devices connected to a network. You can route the IP address which is very useful for internet.

There is 2 categories of IPs:

  • IPv4 (version 4) using 32 binary bits to express the identifier of a device. An IP address version 4 is made of 32 digits which are 0 or 1 (8 digits by group): 4*8 = 32 digits.

Example:

192.168.43.148
  • IPv6 (version 6) using 128 binary bits to express the identifier of a device. IPv6 addresses are divided into 8 groups of 16 digits. Each group is written in hexadecimal. An IP address version 4 is made of 128 digits which are 0 or 1 (16 digits by group): 8*16 = 128 digits.

Example:

2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334

IPv6 has been created because of the growing number of devices connected to the internet, the 232 combinations of IPv4 were not sufficient to cover the new needs of internet (think of IoTs…): IPv6 offers up to 2,128 combinations of IP addresses which expands significantly the number of possible IPs.

Important

In this document we don't focus on IPv6 addresses.

Binary notation for IPv4

IPs are groups of 8 bits to read from right to left for IPv4.

A bit stands for binary digit. The binary system is a number system like decimal system except that binary system uses a base of 2 instead a base of 10.

A bit has two possible values: 0 or 1 and that represents the basic system for computer calculation (your processor works on a sequence of 0 and 1).

Tip

8 bits = 1 Byte. The bits are represented by the b letter and the Bytes by the B letter.

An IPv4 address is a series of 4 groups of numbers separated by a dot. Each group is a 1 octet (8 bits).

Example:

11111111.11111111.11111111.11111111

Here is the table to know how to convert bit to decimal for each group of 8 bits:

Position            7   6   5   4   3   2   1   0
Caculation         2⁷  2⁶  2⁵  2⁴  2³  2²  2¹  2⁰
Result (Decimal)  128  64  32  16   8   4   2   1

Some explanations:

  • You read the groups from right to left.
  • To calculate the 128 decimal value, you calculate 2⁷ = 2222222
  • A group of 8 digits has a maximum 255 decimal values (sum of 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255).

Important

For IP addresses, the maximum number per group of 8 digits is 255. The maximum value is 255.255.255.255.

Example:

We want to convert the following IP:

192.168.1.68

in bits values.

  • 192 = 128 (position 7) + 64 (position 6). So in bits, from right to left, the 1 values are at position 6 and 7 and the others are value 0. The result should be equal to 11000000.
  • 168 = 128 (position 8) + 32 (position 6) + 8 (position 4). The result should be equal to 10101000.
  • 1 = 1 (position 1). The result should be equal to 00000001.
  • 68 = 64 (position 7) + 4 (position 3). The result should be equals to 01000100

The result is:

11000000.10101000.00000001.01000100

IPv4 classes

IPv4 addresses are composed by 2 parts:

  • Network identifier
  • Device identifier

It allows you to define what we call a subnet masks because to divide network in subnets, you must identify in the IP address what identifies the network and what is it specific to an host.

Example:

For a lot of home networks, you have IPs like 192.168.1.20 with subnet masks like 255.255.255.0 (Class C networks). The default notation for such a network is 192.168.1.20/255.255.255.0. But you will see that there will be another notation more concise later.

IPv4 are divided in 4 IP classes. The class of an IP address determines how the address is allocated and how it is used. It defines also the subnet mask that fixes the size of the network.

Important

The last IP address of the network X.X.X.255 is normally reserved to the broadcasting so it is not assignable to an host. The last IP available for an host is consequently X.X.X.254. For example, the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) requests to make the mapping between IPs and MACs are sent using broadcasting.

For IPs Class A:

  • 0 + 7 bits for network + 24 bits for hosts
  • (1 bit = 0) + (2⁷ = 128 networks) + (2²⁴ = 16777216 hosts)

For IPs Class B:

  • 10 + 14 bits for network + 16 bits for hosts
  • (2 bits = 10) + (2¹⁴ = 16384 networks) + (2¹⁶ = 65535 hosts)

For IPs Class C:

  • 110 + 21 bits for network + 8 bits for hosts
  • (3 bits = 110) + (2²¹ = 2097152 networks) + (2⁸ = 256 hosts)

For IPs Class D:

  • 1110 + 28 bits for hosts
  • (4 bits = 1110) + ²²⁸ = 268435456 host

Info

IP classes are no longer widely used, as they have been replaced by Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR). Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) is a method of allocating IP addresses that allows for more flexible and efficient use of IP addresses than the traditional IP classes. With CIDR, IP addresses are assigned to networks in blocks of any size, rather than being pre-allocated to specific classes. This allows for networks of all sizes to be accommodated, from large enterprise networks to small home networks. More about CIDR:

  • RFC 1518: An IAB Consensus Statement
  • RFC 1519: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR): an Address Allocation for the Internet
  • RFC 4632: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR): The IETF Standard (obsoletes RFC 1519)

Important

The CIDR brings a new king of notation, more concise to include subnet masks to IP addresses.

Example:

Instead of the full notation 192.168.1.20/255.255.255.0, you can use the concise representation such as 192.168.1.20/24, meaning that the network is using 24 digits and the hosts 8 digits. 8 digits is 256 hosts. You will see that later in this article.

Gateways

Gateways exist because they allow devices (IP addresses) from different subnets to communicate.

A Gateway is a device with several NICs that communicates with several subnets and acts as messenger between subnets, inline with the Client-Server model (model not described here).

Subnet masks

Subnet masks are always written from left to right with value 255 or 0, but you can have a combination between 255 and 0 and you can't start with 0.

Example:

255.0.0.0 -> Correct 255.255.255.0 -> Correct 255.0.255.255.0 -> Not correct ! 0.0.255.255 -> Not Correct ! 0.255.255.255 -> Not Correct!

As started in IPv4 address description, the subnet mask is associated to an IP address to define:

  • the set of digits representing the network (network identifier)
  • what device you can communicate with

Example:

If you take an IP address 192.168.1.29 associated with the subnet mask 255.255.255.0. So any device compliant to this subnet mask is able to communicate to 192.168.1.29. A device with 192.168.1.13 is able to communicate with 192.168.1.29. A device with 42.51.82.3 is not able to communicate with 192.168.1.29 except using a Gateway.

So, subnet mask defines, for a specific NIC, the range of IP addresses to communicate with. For other IP adresses, the NIC must pass through a Gateway.

Practicing: subnetting by number of subnet

To calculate the adapted mask to your need (the number of subnets you need), the formula is the following:

S = 2^n
  • S = number of expected subnets
  • n = number of masked bits (not really masked in fact but with value 1)

Example:

Imagine you want to create 30 subnets in the 120.0.0.0 network with mask 255.0.0.0. Applying the formula:

2⁰ = 0
2² = 4
2³ = 8
2⁴ = 16
2⁵ = 32   <- Here is enough to contain 30 subnets. So 5 digits are reserved to                the network

In binary, it should be written like this:

  • 11111111 is equivalent to 2⁷ + 2⁶ + 2⁵ + 2⁴ + 2³ + 2² + 2¹ = 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255
  • 11111000 is equivalent to 2⁷ + 2⁶ + 2⁵ + 2⁴ + 2³ = 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 = 248
  • 00000000 is equivalent to 0

Finally the new subnet mask is 255.248.0.0:

  • s = subnet digit
  • h = host digit

meaning 255.248.0.0 and you can calculate the limits of subnets: 256–248 = 8. So the interval separating the subnets is 8 making networks:

Great, you can now create your own subnets based on the subnet number you want.

Note

This method of subnetting is less used than the next method. So we won't develop it more here.

Practicing: subnetting by number of hosts

To calculate the adapted mask to your need (the number of hosts you need), the formula is the following:

S = 2^n - 2
  • S = Number of hosts by subnet
  • n = number of masked bits (not really masked in fact but with value 1)

Example 1:

Imagine you want to create 1800 hosts by subnet in the 192.37.0.0 network with mask 255.255.0.0. Applying the formula:

...
2¹⁰ - 2 = 1022
2¹¹ - 2 = 2046 <-- Here is enough to contain 1800 hosts. So 11 digits are
                   reserved to the hosts

In binary, it should be written like this:

  • 11111111 is equivalent to 2⁷ + 2⁶ + 2⁵ + 2⁴ + 2³ + 2² + 2¹ = 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255
  • 11111000 is equivalent to 2⁷ + 2⁶ + 2⁵ + 2⁴ + 2³ = 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 = 248
  • 00000000 is equivalent to 0

Finally the new subnet mask is 255.255.248.0:

  • s = subnet digit
  • h = host digit

meaning 255.255.248.0 and you can calculate the limits of subnets: 256–248 = 8. So the interval separating the subnets is 8 making networks:

Great, you can now create your own subnets based on the hosts per subnet you want.

Example 2:

We need to create 14 hosts subnets for a local network 192.168.1.0/255.255.255.0.

So 2⁴ -2 = 14 means we need 4 free digits for hosts:

11111111.11111111.11111111.11110000

2⁷ + 2⁶ + 2⁵ + 2⁴ = 128 + 64 + 32+ 16 = 240. 256–240 = 16 which is the range for subnets.

Notation

The conventions to write subnet masks are easy to understand and they are 2:

  • classic notation: You associate the IP with its network mask associated <ip>/<mask>. For example 192.168.1.18/255.255.255.0. This is an obsolete notation
  • CIDR notation: This notation is the most used: you associate to the IP address the number of digits used by the mask. For example, 192.168.1.18/24 means you reserve 24 digits for mask so 8 digits for hosts

Conclusion

Now you are able to design subnets to organize as best as possible the IPs. Your are also able to understand IP notation with their masks.

Hope you will find a practical usage of this article!
